sections.b: The letter opens with eyewitness testimony to "the word of life" that was heard, seen and touched (1:1-4), declares that God is light (1:5) and that God is love (4:8, 16), and gives tests for telling true faith from false: keeping God's commands, loving the brothers, and confessing Jesus Christ come in the flesh. It was written after a group "went out from us" (2:19), and its stated purpose is assurance: "so that you will know that you have eternal life" (5:13). It ends without a farewell: "Little children, guard yourselves against idols" (5:21).

2 John repeats 1 John's key lines in brief: the command "from the beginning" to love each other (1 John 2:7-8; 2 John 5), the deceivers who do not confess Jesus Christ as come or coming in the flesh (1 John 4:1-3; 2 John 7), the antichrist and remaining in the teaching (1 John 2:18-23; 2 John 7-9), and joy "filled up" (1 John 1:4; 2 John 12). Where the Greek is the same, the site's Plain is the same.

common: The letter is widely read as an answer to people who denied that Jesus truly came in the flesh, whether docetists or followers of a teaching like that of Cerinthus.
uncommon: Terry Griffith argues that the opponents were Jewish believers going back to Judaism, and that the question was whether Jesus is the Messiah (2:22).

sections.b: The word itself comes from 1 John. The readers had "heard that antichrist is coming", but the letter's surprise is that "many antichrists have arisen" already: teachers who had left the church (2:18-19). The antichrist is "the one who denies the Father and the Son" (2:22), and every spirit that does not confess Jesus belongs to the antichrist, which is "in the world already" (4:3; compare 2 John 7). The letter uses the word of a kind of person and a power at work now, not as the name of one future ruler.

common: Many Christians expect one final Antichrist and read John's "many antichrists" as his forerunners.
uncommon: Others read 1 John as saying that antichrist is any denial of Jesus come in the flesh, in every age, with no single end-time figure in view.

sections.b: 1 John calls Jesus the hilasmos where our sins are concerned and adds, "it is for the whole world" (2:2); it also says God "sent his Son to be the atoning sacrifice where our sins are concerned" (4:10). The Greek Old Testament uses hilasmos for the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 25:9) and the ram of atonement (Numbers 5:8). The KJV's "propitiation" stresses turning away God's anger; "expiation" stresses wiping away sin (the English Catholic Catechism uses it in quoting 4:10). The letter puts the sacrifice inside God's love: "It is not that we have loved God; it is that he himself loved us" (4:10). 2:2 is also a key text in the debate over whom Christ died for: see the card on 1 John 2.
sections.refs: 1 John 1:7; 1 John 2:1-2; 1 John 4:9-10; Leviticus 25:9; Numbers 5:8; Romans 3:25

sections.h: 1 John: the Father, the Son and the Spirit
sections.b: 1 John speaks of fellowship "with the Father, and with his Son Jesus Christ" (1:3), says that denying the Son means not having the Father (2:23), and knows God's presence by "the Spirit he has given us" (3:24; 4:13). It ends by saying of Jesus Christ, "This one is the real God and eternal life" (5:20), though some read "this one" as the Father. The KJV's "three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost" (5:7, KJV) is a later Latin addition, not part of the original letter: see the Johannine Comma page. Greek fathers who set out the doctrine in the 300s, such as Athanasius and Basil, never quote the added words.

In Greek the added words appear first in a Greek translation of the Acts of the Lateran Council of 1215, then in a handful of late manuscripts: 629 (1300s-1400s), 918 (1500s), 61 (Codex Montfortianus, about 1520, translated from the Latin), 2473 (1600s) and 2318 (1700s), and as later notes in the margins of a few more. In Latin they appear first in the Liber Apologeticus (about 380, probably by Priscillian), then in Spanish Old Latin copies and later Vulgate manuscripts, but not in the two oldest Vulgate manuscripts, Fuldensis (546) and Amiatinus. Cyprian (died 258) wrote of Father, Son and Spirit, "And these three are one", but scholars disagree whether he was quoting the added words or reading the Trinity into 5:8.

The Complutensian Polyglot printed the words in Greek and Latin in its New Testament of 1514, but that work was not published until 1520-1521. Erasmus left the words out of his Greek New Testament of 1516 and 1519 and added them in 1522, after being accused of reviving Arianism and being told of a Greek manuscript that had them, while voicing doubts in his notes; the story that he had promised to do so has been questioned (H. J. de Jonge, 1980). Luther's German New Testament, made from the 1519 edition, lacked them; the KJV of 1611 printed them. Isaac Newton wrote against them to John Locke in 1690. The Catholic Holy Office ruled in 1897 that their authenticity could not safely be denied; in 1927 the question was opened to investigation, and the Nova Vulgata leaves them out. English Bibles made from the critical text have left them out of the main text since 1881.

common: Many readers know the words from the KJV, which printed them from 1611 on.
uncommon: A minority, chiefly defenders of the Textus Receptus and the KJV, hold that the words are original and were lost from the Greek.

sections.b: "God is light, and in him there is no darkness, not the least bit" (1:5). The letter turns the picture into a test: to claim fellowship with God while walking in darkness is a lie (1:6); hating a brother is darkness, and it blinds (2:9-11); loving him is remaining in the light (2:10). The darkness "is passing away, and the real light already shines" (2:8). The Community Rule from Qumran also speaks of "the spirits of truth and falsehood" and of children of light ruled by "the Prince of Light" (Community Rule, column 3, lines 18-21, in Vermes's translation), but there the line is drawn by God's plan; in 1 John it shows in how people love.

1 John says twice, "God is love" (4:8, 16), and defines that love by an act: "God has sent his only Son into the world so that we may live through him" (4:9), "to be the atoning sacrifice where our sins are concerned" (4:10). Love for God is shown in keeping his commands (5:3) and above all in loving the brother one can see (4:20). "We love because he loved us first" (4:19), and "Complete love throws fear out" (4:18). Augustine drew from this letter his saying "Love, and do what you will" (Homilies on 1 John 7.8).

common: "God is love" (1 John 4:8) is among the most quoted verses of the Bible.

sections.b: 1 John calls the command to love "old", because it goes back to the beginning and to Leviticus 19:18, and "new", because Jesus gave it as "a new command" (John 13:34). It makes love for the brother the test of being in the light (2:9-11), of having passed from death to life (3:14), and of loving God at all (4:20-21). Love shares goods with a brother in need (3:17), as the Torah forbids closing one's hand to him (Deuteronomy 15:7).
sections.refs: 1 John 2:7-11; 1 John 3:11-18; 1 John 4:20-21; Leviticus 19:17-18; Deuteronomy 15:7; John 13:34

sections.b: 1 John speaks of being "born from God" ten times. The new birth shows in a family likeness: whoever does righteousness (2:29), loves (4:7) and believes that Jesus is the Messiah (5:1) has been born from God; the one born from God "does not sin" because God's seed remains in him (3:9; 5:18), and wins the victory over the world (5:4). The Gospel's words stand behind it (John 1:12-13; John 3:3-8).

sections.h: The anointing all believers have (1 John 2:20, 27)
sections.b: Against the antichrists, the readers "have an anointing, which comes from the Holy One" (2:20), and it "teaches you about all things" (2:27). The word chrisma plays on Christos, the Anointed One, and antichristos. Readers take it as the Holy Spirit, the gospel word, or both; the Orthodox Church cites 2:20 for chrismation, the anointing after baptism.

1 John says that we know God remains in us "from the Spirit he has given us" (3:24; 4:13), and in the same breath tells the readers to test every spirit by its confession: "any spirit that confesses Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh is from God" (4:2). The Spirit of truth stands against "the spirit that leads astray" (4:6), and the Spirit is one of the three witnesses with the water and the blood (5:6-8). In the letter the Advocate is Jesus (2:1); in the Gospel it is the Spirit (John 14:16).

"Not as Cain was: he was from the evil one, and he slaughtered his brother" (1 John 3:12). The letter gives the reason Genesis leaves unsaid: Cain's deeds were evil and Abel's righteous. It makes Cain the pattern of hatred, which is murder (3:15), against Christ, who laid down his life (3:16). Later Jewish retellings went further and made Cain the child of an angel or of Sammael (Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 4:1; Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 21).

1 John calls Satan "the evil one" and "the devil". The young men have won the victory over him (2:13-14); the devil "has been sinning from the beginning", and "the Son of God appeared: to undo the works of the devil" (3:8); the one born from God is safe from him, though "the world, all of it, lies in the evil one's hands" (5:18-19). "Greater is the one in you than the one in the world" (4:4).

Only 1 John says "it is the last hour", and its proof is the appearance of many antichrists (2:18). The darkness is passing and the real light already shines (2:8); the world is passing away (2:17); Christ's coming is awaited (2:28; 3:2). Readers take "the last hour" as the short time before the return, as the whole age between Christ's two comings, or as the crisis of this church.

1 John holds two sayings together: "If we say, 'We have no sin,' we are leading ourselves astray" (1:8), and "Anyone who remains in him does not sin" (3:6; 3:9; 5:18). It defines sin as "lawlessness" (3:4) and "All unrighteousness is sin" (5:17), and it distinguishes sin "headed toward death" from sin that is not (5:16-17). The remedy is confession, the blood of Jesus, and the Advocate who is the atoning sacrifice (1:7-2:2). See the deep dive on 1 John 3 and the card on 1 John 5.

1 John 3:6-9 says that whoever remains in God "does not sin" and "cannot sin". John Wesley built his teaching on Christian perfection on such verses: "A Christian is so far perfect, as not to commit sin" (Sermon 40), meaning willful sin; Lutheran, Reformed and Catholic teaching hold that the believer, though truly made holy, still sins in this life (Smalcald Articles 3.3; Westminster Confession 13.2; Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 11). See the card on 1 John 3.

sections.h: The sin headed toward death (1 John 5:16-17)
sections.b: 1 John tells believers to pray for a brother whose sin is "not headed toward death", but says of "sin headed toward death", "I am not saying he should make a request about that" (5:16). Readers take it as apostasy and the denial of Christ (Calvin; Wesley), as mortal sin (the Catholic Catechism, paragraph 1854), as a sin punished by bodily death (Acts 5:1-11; 1 Corinthians 11:30), or in light of the Torah's sins "with a high hand" (Numbers 15:30). It is often compared with the blasphemy against the Spirit (Mark 3:28-29).

"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and he is just: he will forgive us our sins and make us clean from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9). The confession is spoken to God, as Israel confessed on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:21) and the psalmist did (Psalm 32:5). Calvin used the verse to argue that confession is owed to God; the practice of confession to a priest rests mainly on John 20:23 and James 5:16.
sections.refs: 1 John 1:7-9; 1 John 2:1-2, 12; Leviticus 16:21; Psalm 32:5; John 20:23; James 5:16

sections.b: 1 John gives a confession test: "any spirit that confesses Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh is from God, and any spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God" (4:2-3). The false prophets had gone out from the church (2:19; 4:1), the world listens to them (4:5), and the readers do not need their teaching, because the anointing teaches them (2:27). 2 John adds a practical rule: do not take such a teacher into the house (2 John 10).

sections.h: "We will see him just as he is" (1 John)
sections.b: "No one has ever gazed at God" (1 John 4:12), yet the writer has gazed at and touched "the word of life" (1:1), and the letter promises that when he appears "we will be like him, since we will see him just as he is" (3:2). The Catholic Catechism cites 3:2 for the vision of God in heaven (paragraphs 163, 1023). In the meantime the unseen God is present where believers love each other (4:12).

Orthodox writers cite 1 John 3:2 for theosis, "real union with God", alongside 2 Peter 1:4; John Wesley wrote that the promise "will raise the children of God to be, in a manner, as God himself". The letter adds the moral side at once: "everyone who has this hope set on him makes himself pure" (3:3).

1 John ends abruptly: "Little children, guard yourselves against idols." Readers take the idols as the temples and images of the cities of Asia, as the false god of the opponents' teaching set against "the real God" of 5:20, or as anything put in God's place.

1 John was known by Polycarp and Papias, quoted as John's by Irenaeus and by Clement of Alexandria (who called it John's "larger Epistle"), and listed by Eusebius among the books acknowledged by all, while 2 and 3 John were among the disputed (Church History 3.24.17; 3.25.2-3).

sections.h: 1 John: an early papyrus and a late addition
sections.b: Among the earliest surviving copies of 1 John is Papyrus 9, a carelessly written leaf of the 200s from Oxyrhynchus with parts of 4:11-17. At the other end of the story stands the Johannine Comma (5:7-8), Latin words that were printed in Greek in the Complutensian Polyglot (printed 1514, published 1520-1521) and in Erasmus' third edition (1522), and in English in the KJV of 1611. Since 2012 the critical text of 1 John in NA28 has come from the Editio Critica Maior (first published for 1 John in 2003), which changed four readings (1:7; 3:7; 5:10; 5:18).

1 John names no writer. Irenaeus quotes it as the letter of John, the disciple of the Lord; Eusebius preserves Papias' mention of two Johns, the apostle and "the presbyter John", and reports two tombs called John's at Ephesus (Church History 3.39.5-7). Modern scholars divide between the apostle, John the Elder and a circle of John's disciples; most think the three letters have one author, but there is no consensus that he also wrote the Gospel.

1 John shares the Gospel's vocabulary on almost every line, and most scholars agree that one borrows directly from the other. Both open with "beginning" and the life that was with God (John 1:1-4; 1 John 1:1-2); both give a purpose sentence (John 20:31; 1 John 5:13). The letter calls Jesus the Advocate (1 John 2:1), where the Gospel calls the Spirit "another Advocate" (John 14:16).

sections.h: "They were never really from us" (1 John 2:19)
sections.b: 1 John says of those who left, "Had they been from us, they would have remained with us" (2:19). Some read this as showing that those who finally fall away were never true believers; others read it as the history of one split, not a rule for every case. The letter's purpose is assurance: "so that you will know that you have eternal life" (5:13).

In 1 John the confession that Jesus is the Messiah is the mark of the one born from God (5:1), and denying it is the lie of the antichrist (2:22). The letter plays on the title: believers have an anointing (chrisma) from the Holy One, against the anti-anointed (antichristoi) who left (2:18-27).
